sections.title: Profile
sections.text: Crackborne, real name Tanya. Formerly a laborer of Zelgrad, Ursus, where she launched a resistance movement under the name of 'Reunion.' She was later introduced to Rhodes Island by Crownslayer to receive treatment, and now takes part in Rhodes Island's field operations as a full Operator.

sections.title: Clinical Analysis
sections.text:
Imaging tests show the indistinct outlines of internal organs, obscured by abnormal shadows. Originium granules detected in the circulatory system. The subject is confirmed to be infected with Oripathy.

[Cell-Originium Assimilation] 3.5%
Trace amounts of Originium crystals are distributed across the surface of Operator Crackborne's body.

[Blood Originium-Crystal Density] 0.17u/L
Operator Crackborne has a strong awareness of Oripathy protection, and as she has long engaged in heavy physical labor, both her physical qualities and her physical resilience are above average.

sections.title: Archive File 1
sections.text:
Tanya was born on a construction site in Zelgrad. Her mother was an optimistic, diligent construction worker; her father, a silent and embittered firefighter. On the day Tanya was born, her father rode his bicycle to the site, found that her mother had already been wheeled out of the makeshift delivery room, said a single 'Good,' then got back on his bicycle and left.
In Zelgrad, the children of construction workers do not go to school. Looking after her little brothers and sisters naturally became Tanya's task. Tanya liked to stare into their eyes—she always felt something very special was hidden in there, though she could never work out what it was.
Her mother died not long after giving birth to her fifth child—Nina. At the moment she leapt from the ten-story staff dormitory, Tanya was sitting by the corridor railing, stacking a pile of empty detergent cans into the shape of a tower block.
After her mother's death, her father grew even more silent, and all the housework fell on Tanya. She never complained; as she saw it, if she didn't cook she would starve, and if she didn't do the laundry there would be no clean clothes to wear—so it was nothing. One night, her father suddenly dragged her out of bed, and, meeting her terrified eyes, said in a trembling voice, 'I'm taking you to see the fire.'
By then her father had long since been struck off the fire brigade's rolls and had sunk into drunkenness, yet that night he moved as nimbly as he had in his youth. All but dragging Tanya along, he raced up a hill made of construction spoil, then climbed a stretch of unfinished city wall. At last he pointed at the firelight flickering endlessly within that towering stone wall and said to Tanya, 'It's burning over there. They're burning! Everyone's finished!' Then he laughed and laughed, until he collapsed on the ground and curled up in a ball.
The restless firelight leapt over the stone wall, and its shifting colors held Tanya spellbound. The next moment she heard the whistling of crossbow bolts behind the wall, heard the cold commands coming through the loudspeakers, and woke from her trance. Tanya ran all the way home. Her brothers and sisters were still sleeping soundly. In her panic she climbed into bed and sang herself a lullaby.
Her father died only a few days after the Patrol Unit dumped him back home; the cause was most likely liver disease. Tanya tried to find out why that firelight had appeared behind the stone wall that night, but no one could give her an answer. The wall was as silent as her father.
On the day the powdered milk tin ran empty, she took her mother's bloodstained work clothes to the construction site. A junior foreman pulled her aside and said a great many things, the gist of which was this: every city in Ursus is built this way. Construction workers put down roots on empty land, becoming the first residents of the new city; they build their city with their own hands, and yet they will never deserve a home of their own. The point of the stone wall is to block every prying gaze—it was built that way not only for practicality, but to frighten anyone who would not stay in their place. Only after Tanya promised she would never again ask about anything behind the wall did the foreman press a powdered-milk voucher into her hand.
That voucher, in the end, bought only a bag of coarse salt; powdered milk was scarce everywhere. Carrying the salt home, she passed by the stone wall and wondered: what on earth was she supposed to do with a bag of salt? She thought of her siblings crying from hunger, of the shriveled muscles and glistening beads of sweat on the workers at the site, of her father's mad laughter, of the firelight that night, of the glimmer she had seen the first time she looked into her siblings' eyes—
A shaft of sunlight spilled down past the top of the stone wall and fell less than a meter in front of her; she needed only to take one small step more to walk into that light. In that moment she understood why she had thought of children's eyes, the color of fire, falling beads of sweat, powdered milk, or salt... That was life. That was living—whatever kind of living it turned out to be. And so she lifted her head and went forward to meet it.
She still loves that numb, unbearably painful life.

sections.title: Archive File 2
sections.text:
Operator Crackborne's record for jobs worked in a single day at Rhodes Island is twelve—slightly below her record back in Zelgrad, by her own account. 'Working jobs' is neither an accurate nor a sufficiently formal description: the paid volunteer services she performs at Rhodes Island, or serving as a test subject in drug trials that pay in nutrient-supplement vouchers, do not strictly count as employment. Even so, 'working jobs' really is the phrase that best describes Crackborne's condition.
Crackborne's schedule is usually divided into fifteen-minute units, and some of her jobs even overlap. Which is why someone once saw her preparing sports drinks for one team in the Rhodes Island Operator Basketball League, then suddenly pull out the rival team's fan banner and start cheering them on.
Even Crackborne's only rest period during the day overlaps with something else on her schedule—according to the Medical Department, the moment Crackborne lies down on a bed she falls asleep at once, and neither injections nor wound debridement will disturb her. When the treatment is over and the alarm she set in advance goes off, she wakes without the slightest reluctance, gets up and leaves, and hurries off to wherever her next odd job awaits.
Crackborne has her reasons. Anyone who knows her can easily see how much she loves her little brothers and sisters. She always arrives at the children's ward five minutes early, waiting for them to finish their treatment, walk out of the room, and hug her. For those five minutes, she does nothing at all.
When she first joined, Human Resources applied on her behalf for every subsidy she was eligible for, which broadly covered the medical expenses of both herself and her siblings. As her length of service grew, the various employee benefits were extended to her one after another. So when HR discovered during a follow-up interview that she was still 'working jobs' at such intensity, their first reaction was to apply for a special medical assistance program on her behalf. This time, however, Crackborne said that there was no longer any shortfall in the medical expenses for herself and her siblings, that their quality of life was steadily improving, and that such assistance programs should go to people who needed them more.
'But then,' the HR Operator asked, 'why do you still work so hard at all those side jobs?'
Crackborne answered as follows:
'I want to buy a skirt. I don't wear skirts, and I don't like them, but I want to own one. I don't care about the pattern, the style, or the price, because I'll almost certainly never wear it my whole life. But I want to have one. I'll earn the money myself, and I'll buy it myself. It doesn't have to actually be a skirt, but I have to own it.'
Operator Crackborne said it with absolute finality, as though she meant to buy an entire nation, or the happiness of an ordinary person's whole life.

sections.title: Archive File 3
sections.text:
[Lawn Mower]
Definition: A mechanical device powered by Originium energy that uses high-frequency vibrating blades (or energy streams) to cut away excess vegetation.
Example: I had meant to mow the yard with the lawn mower this afternoon, but then I saw how the sunlight had warmed every single blade of grass on the lawn, and decided to just let them go on growing as freely as they liked.
Your turn: (in crooked handwriting) The yard downstairs from my home has nothing but piles of sand and gravel—no grass, and no lawn mower. We use chainsaws, bulldozers, and fire to clear away excess vegetation.

[Oath]
Definition: A promise carrying a certain binding force, founded upon a person's words, deeds, or Originium Arts. Generally speaking, both making an oath and breaking one are choices of the utmost importance, and sometimes the significance of the choice itself outweighs the content of the oath.
Example: At the wedding they read out their respective vows. The guests had no way of knowing whether the newlyweds would keep to those vows in the future, but they were willing to applaud and cheer for that moment all the same.
Your turn: (a single question mark)

[Family Gathering]
Definition: A gathering held by family unit, usually on important holidays or during festivities. The 'family' here does not specifically refer to the 'Siracusan famiglia' of the previous entry; please note the distinction.
Example: Tired of the crowded, tedious family gatherings, he decided that this year he would just mail a greeting card home and let it attend in his place.
Your turn: (left completely blank)

[Dessert]
Definition: High-sugar foods enjoyed after the main meal, such as muffins, crème caramel, or scoops of ice cream.
Example: I deliberately ate a few fewer cuts of meat to save room for dessert.
Your turn: (a crossed-out 'Why?') If dessert is part of the meal too, then calling it an 'after-meal' dessert doesn't make any sense.

Crackborne cut a few common-word entries out of her literacy textbook and tucked them inside the cover of her Operator pass, so that she could take them out and memorize them at any time.
To her, these are things that resist classification, lying somewhere between what she once had, what she longs to have, and what she cannot understand.

The 'lawn mower' one is an exception. I just find that example sentence comforting. I like it.
—Crackborne

sections.title: Archive File 4
sections.text:
Zelgrad:
I'm writing you a letter. You aren't a person, but you are the name I know best, and apart from that name I couldn't think of any way to begin this letter 'to the one I know best.'
In literacy class, the teacher compared the motherland and one's hometown to a mother, but I never once saw you that way. Once, I thought of you as my friend. When I was born, your stone wall was already half-built; the way I saw it, you and I grew up together, so of course we ought to be friends.
But later I realized that you didn't know me. I would secretly carve letters into the stone wall, and by the next day the marks would be gone—you could never remember me. From then on, I stopped thinking of you as a friend.
You were like a stranger living in my house who never spoke to me. When I laughed, you couldn't see it; when I cried, you couldn't hear it; and if I had cursed at you, I doubt you would have reacted at all. Back then I thought you were arrogant. Your stone wall was taller than a hundred of me stacked up, and even if you had been willing to speak, I figured it would take a whole day for the sound to reach the bottom. So I decided to stop trying to understand you.
Then, later, Nina died.
One person's death can change a great many things, because with their death that person changes the people who are still alive—changes their thoughts, changes the way they look at things.
I was changed.
I saw the stains that wouldn't wash out. I saw that the stone wall had gaps in it after all. I saw that under the daily wind and rain and sun, even the stone wall grows cracks.
Zelgrad, that was when I saw it clearly: the people inside the stone wall, what they were doing was destroying you. And the only way to save you—to save my two sisters and one brother who hadn't died yet, to save myself, to save everyone else in the city—would destroy you all the same.
Selfishly, I thought: if you were doomed to be destroyed anyway, then you ought to be destroyed by the hands of the very people who built you.
To this day I still remember that day—clutching Nina's swaddling cloth, listening to the shells flying overhead, knowing that you were dying.
I left you, Zelgrad. And only as I was leaving did I realize that you weren't the stranger living in my house—you were the home.
How could I have been so slow to see it?
Zelgrad, you are already dead. But one day I will go back to see you.
I'll come to see you carrying sand, soil, and tree seeds, because back when neither you nor I had been born, the first people to stand on that land had nothing but these things either.
Your friend, your builder, your family, and the one who destroyed you
Tanya

sections.title: Promotion Record
sections.text:
[A Salute to the Undefeated Sparring Partner]
Thanks for coming to help me test 'Tooty'! As a thank-you, I've written my proudest work on the back of this postcard—my improved recipe for Rim Billiton truck stew! Potlid says you can ask her whenever you run into trouble. Can't be helped—she's the real chef around here.

[Happy Birthday, Masha]
Masha said last time that the desserts I make are delicious, so today I baked a birthday cake in that very same flavor. Happy birthday to the little one. Also, I know you're a bit of a clean freak, so rest assured—I made it in a toxin-free bakery, and the blue coloring in the cake is natural jam, which isn't toxic either.

[Thank You for Yielding]
Thank you for letting me have that volume of pastoral poetry at the library. For two people to pick out the very same book at the same time is a marvelous coincidence in itself, and your courtesy let me feel a kind of beauty that needs no explaining. I noticed that you had also borrowed some romance novels and tales of chivalry; if it interests you, I would like to invite you to a reading club.

Before she knew it, Crackborne had amassed a whole cookie tin's worth of postcards. Unfortunately, back when she first started receiving gifts and cards from other Operators, she couldn't read many characters yet, and was too embarrassed to take a card to someone and ask what it meant—writing back was out of the question.
After a long time at Rhodes Island, Crackborne gradually came to realize that the way she had behaved back then might have seemed rude. So she began reading and replying to those cards, one by one.
The most recent one she received was an invitation to a social dance, and sure enough, the date written on it had already passed several weeks before. This sort of thing had happened many times, but perhaps because she had just written so many words, Crackborne was suddenly seized by a regret she had never felt before.
She wasn't very used to that feeling.
After entrusting someone to send out all of her written replies at once, she hesitantly sent a message on her terminal to the organizer of that social dance, apologizing in the most sincere words she knew and cautiously asking whether there would be more dances in the future.
Almost the instant the message went out, there was a knock at her dorm room door. Crackborne opened it, and an Operator with a gentle smile said softly what a coincidence it was—she had happened to be passing Crackborne's dorm just as the message arrived, and what was more, she had been about to set off for tonight's social dance. And then that Operator held out her hand to Crackborne.
